maintainer_feedback.author: jimvixx
maintainer_feedback.body:
Thank you for the contribution and for testing SMSecure with RVSec!

I reviewed the proposed change. According to the Android documentation, `HmacSHA1` is a supported `KeyGenerator` algorithm, so the reported violation may be related to the CrySL rule rather than an actual Android API issue.

Also, the generated key material is subsequently used with `HmacSHA1` throughout the existing MasterSecret implementation. Switching only the key generator to `HmacSHA256` does not change the MAC algorithm or provide a direct security improvement.

Could you share the exact CrySL rule violation and explain why `HmacSHA1` is considered invalid in this context?

I'd prefer to preserve the existing cryptographic behavior unless there is a demonstrated issue. Adding an explicit 160-bit initialization to the current `HmacSHA1` generator might be a simpler alternative.

Thanks again for investigating this!

maintainer_feedback.author: javalc6
maintainer_feedback.body:
Thanks for taking the time to run the app under RVSec, but it will not be merged. In _FileManager_, MD5 is used only as a checksum to detect accidental corruption of a backup file. It isn’t used for authentication, signatures, or password hashing, so MD5’s known weaknesses (collision attacks) don’t apply here. 

Since there’s no secret key, switching to SHA-256 wouldn’t stop anyone from modifying a file and recomputing a valid checksum, so it wouldn’t improve security. 

The _MessageDigestSpec_ warning is a generic rule that flags MD5 regardless of how it’s used. Note that _MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5")_ isn’t rejected by the Java/Android API [MessageDigest](https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/MessageDigest)

maintainer_feedback.author: mpretty-cyro
maintainer_feedback.body:
Thanks for your PR @jpantonow, I took a look at the change and on Android, `SSLContext.getInstance("SSL")` and `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` resolve to the same implementation. Conscrypt registers "SSL" as an alias of "TLS" (https://github.com/google/conscrypt/blob/5bdcae0fe8aeb92009eba087969aed7f0ae0e167/common/src/main/java/org/conscrypt/OpenSSLProvider.java#L92-L94), and the negotiated protocol version is set by OkHttp's `ConnectionSpec` on each connection rather than by this string.

So this change doesn't alter runtime behaviour; it only satisfies the CrySL `SSLContextSpec` rule. We'll hold off merging for now since it doesn't change anything functionally.

maintainer_feedback.author: mpretty-cyro
maintainer_feedback.body: All good, happy to merge it - just wanted to flag that it doesn't impact security in case someone read the PR and misunderstood

maintainer_feedback.author: ibrahim-iqbal
maintainer_feedback.body:
Read this carefully — the fix is right, and the delegate approach is the cleanest way to do it.

**Context for anyone reading this later:** `trustAllCerts` is Feeder's user-opt-in helper for self-hosted servers with weird cert setups (self-signed, custom CA, mismatched hostname). The tightening here doesn't change what it accepts on the trust side — it changes what protocols the resulting `SSLSocketFactory` will speak. `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` on Android/JVM initialises the context correctly but leaves legacy TLSv1/TLSv1.1 (and, historically, SSLv2/v3) in each socket's `enabledProtocols`. `droidbot:dfs_naive` caught that.

What lands:

- `ProtocolFilteringSslSocketFactory` wraps every socket the delegate creates, then strips anything matching `SSL*`, `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.0`, `TLSv1.1` from `enabledProtocols`. What survives is TLS 1.2/1.3, which is exactly the tool's expectation.
- `filterLegacyTlsProtocols` throws `IOException` if the filter would empty the array — fail-secure rather than silently disable TLS entirely. Good.
- Wrapping is preferred over calling `SSLContext.getInstance("TLSv1.3")` because Android's min-API surface still varies on TLS 1.3 availability, and the delegate model keeps `NoSuchAlgorithmException` handling out of hot paths.
- All seven `createSocket` overloads are covered, including the `(socket, host, port, autoClose)` layered variant that OkHttp actually uses. If any of those had been missed, the wrapper would silently return an un-filtered socket for that code path.
- The `configure` closer-on-failure block preserves the filtering exception rather than swallowing it under a `close()` failure. Nice detail.

Small observations, non-blocking:

- `isLegacyTlsProtocol` uses `ignoreCase = true` — matches historical `TLSv1` vs `TLSv1.0` naming quirks across JDK vendors, so this is defensive not paranoid.
- The added androidTest exercises the filter directly; a wider integration test asserting a real TLSv1.2-only handshake would be nice-to-have

maintainer_feedback.author: Copilot
maintainer_feedback.body: Wrapping the global HttpsURLConnection default SSLSocketFactory unconditionally in the constructor can lead to wrapper stacking if RESTMusicService is instantiated more than once, and it makes the global TLS behavior dependent on object construction order. Guard against double-wrapping so subsequent instances don’t keep nesting factories.

maintainer_feedback.author: Copilot
maintainer_feedback.body: If legacy-protocol filtering removes all enabled protocols, filterLegacyTlsProtocols throws IllegalStateException, which currently bubbles out of SSLSocketFactory.createSocket(...) as an unchecked exception. That’s surprising for callers expecting an IOException/SSLException from socket creation and can make failures harder to handle consistently; convert this to an SSLException (and still close the socket) when it occurs during socket configuration.
